title: Foods highest in monounsaturated fat

seo.title: Foods highest in monounsaturated fat: ranking and servings
seo.meta_description: Olive oil, macadamias, hazelnuts, pecans, almonds and avocado are rich in monounsaturated fat. Compare per 100 g and realistic servings.
seo.search_intent: Identify foods rich in monounsaturated fats and understand how much a typical serving provides.

excerpt: Oils lead by concentration because they are almost pure fat: olive oil provides roughly 70–75 g of monounsaturated fat per 100 g. Among whole foods, macadamias, hazelnuts, pecans and almonds stand out. In real portions, a tablespoon of olive oil provides about 10 g of monounsaturated fat and an ounce of macadamias about 17 g.
content_html:
If foods are ranked by monounsaturated fat per 100 g, oils inevitably take the top spots because almost all of their weight is fat. That does not make 100 g of avocado and 100 g of oil comparable servings.

The useful comparison needs both concentration and portion size.

Foods that concentrate monounsaturated fat

Monounsaturated fat appears in foods with very different structures, and that changes how the fat enters a meal. Olive oil is almost entirely fat and concentrates a large amount in a spoonful; avocado brings fat with water and fiber; nuts and seeds also add protein, minerals, and texture. Two foods can deliver similar oleic acid yet behave very differently in portion size and satiety. Ranking foods only by grams of monounsaturated fat misses that food matrix, which is often more useful when deciding how a source will fit into the rest of the diet.

FoodMUFA/100 gServingMUFA/serving
Olive oil~73 g1 tbsp (14 g)~10 g
Macadamias~59 g1 oz~17 g
Hazelnuts~46 g1 oz~13 g
Pecans~41 g1 oz~12 g
Almonds~32 g1 oz~9 g
Pistachios~23 g1 oz~6.5 g
Avocado~10 g100 g~10 g

Avocado looks much lower on a 100 g ranking, yet a 100 g portion supplies about as much monounsaturated fat as a tablespoon of olive oil. The avocado also contains water, fiber and structure; oil is concentrated fat.

Oleic acid is the main player

The dominant monounsaturated fatty acid in olive oil is oleic acid. It also makes up a large share of the fat in avocado, macadamias, hazelnuts and almonds.

“Monounsaturated” describes chemical structure—one double bond—not a claim that every food in the table is nutritionally interchangeable.

A serving of nuts can exceed a tablespoon of oil

The nutritional advantage is often about substitution rather than addition. Replacing butter or another saturated-fat-heavy ingredient with olive oil, nuts, or avocado changes the fat profile of a meal. Pouring oil and adding nuts on top of a meal that already met your energy needs is a different choice. That distinction is why “healthy fat” should not be interpreted as unlimited fat. A practical approach is to let monounsaturated-rich foods take the place of less useful fat sources when the recipe and eating pattern make that swap easy.

An ounce of macadamias provides about 17 g of monounsaturated fat, compared with roughly 10 g in a tablespoon of olive oil. The nuts also provide some protein and fiber and about 200 calories; the tablespoon of oil provides roughly 120 calories.

The better choice depends on what role the food plays in the meal, not simply which number is largest.

Monounsaturated does not mean unlimited

Dietary guidance favors replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats, but all fat still provides around 9 calories per gram. Replacing butter with olive oil can improve fat quality; adding oil on top of everything else also raises total energy.

For cooking, oil stability depends on more than the percentage of monounsaturated fat. Refining, natural antioxidants, temperature, and heating time all influence how an oil behaves. There is no need to choose the food with the most oleic acid for every recipe. One oil may be ideal for dressing while another is practical for cooking, and nuts or avocado do not serve the same culinary function at all. Thinking in concrete substitutions—oil in place of butter, nuts in place of a more refined snack—turns a nutrient number into real decisions and avoids pretending that all monounsaturated-fat sources are interchangeable products.

Which sources are easiest to use?

Different sources also solve different kitchen problems. Oil works for dressings and sautéing, nuts add crunch and portability, and avocado can provide body in sandwiches, bowls, or sauces. No single food needs to win an absolute ranking. Rotating several sources adds variety and brings along different micronutrients and textures. When comparing packaged foods, look at the actual serving and total fat rather than relying on a front-of-pack claim about monounsaturated fat. The useful question is how the source changes the whole meal, not whether it tops a list.

Olive oil is a straightforward way to replace more saturated cooking fats. Nuts provide monounsaturated fats in a solid food that also contains fiber and protein. Avocado delivers them with much more water and volume.

There is no single practical winner: the best source depends on what it replaces and how much you use.

faq.question: What food has the most monounsaturated fat?
faq.answer: Oils rich in oleic acid rank highest by weight. Olive oil provides roughly 70–75 g of monounsaturated fat per 100 g.

faq.question: How much monounsaturated fat is in a tablespoon of olive oil?
faq.answer: A 14 g tablespoon provides about 10 g of monounsaturated fat.

faq.question: Is avocado high in monounsaturated fat?
faq.answer: Yes. A 100 g serving provides about 10 g, though avocado contains much more water than oil or nuts.
